definition: Mooers's law is a comment about the use of information retrieval systems made by the American computer scientist Calvin Mooers in 1959: An information retrieval system will tend not to be used whenever it is more painful and troublesome for a customer to have information than for him not to have it.
details: Mooers's law is a comment about the use of information retrieval systems made by the American computer scientist Calvin Mooers in 1959: An information retrieval system will tend not to be used whenever it is more painful and troublesome for a customer to have information than for him not to have it.

explainer.lead: Mooers's law, stated by Calvin Mooers in 1959, says an information retrieval system tends not to be used when having the information is more painful and troublesome than not having it. It matters because usability, not capability, decides adoption.

tiers.eli5: If finding the answer is more hassle than not knowing it, you won't bother looking it up.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply it by weighing the effort of retrieving information against the cost of going without, since users abandon systems whose retrieval is more trouble than it is worth. A pitfall is optimizing retrieval quality while ignoring the friction users feel.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, it is a comment by Calvin Mooers (1959): an information retrieval system will tend not to be used whenever it is more painful and troublesome for a customer to have information than for him not to have it.

explainer.example: A user facing a cumbersome retrieval interface skips it and proceeds without the information, because obtaining it costs more trouble than lacking it.
